AI-based chatbots (n=20) utilized to comprehend user responses and generate replies, versus rule-based approaches with predefined rules. Qualitative feedback highlighted empathic and interactive communication, non-judgment, alliance relationship. human_support: Most chatbots were fully automated. Only 3 studies explicitly integrated human assistance (Bray et al. 2020; Nicol et al. 2022; Russell et al. 2021) and showed lower attrition rates. engagement_features: Safety measures in 14 studies: emergency assistance (n=12), crisis identification (n=6), professional accompaniment (n=2). Embodiment in 8 studies. No specific mention of reminders, gamification, progress indicators, or rewards at review level.
co_design: 11 studies explicitly employed a co-design approach involving end users in chatbot development. title: BetterMood: A human-like AI counseling service for adolescents and young adults.
bibliographic: authors: Do Hyung Kim, Soeun Baek, Joonsung Lee, Taehwi Lee, Soyeon Park, Beomchan You, Ji-Won Hur, Minah Kim, Chang-Gun Lee | year: 2025 | title: BetterMood: A human-like AI counseling service for adolescents and young adults | venue: DIGITAL HEALTH | doi: 10.1177/20552076251392294 | publication_type: Original research article
sample_size: n: 128 | basis: Enrolled: 10 adolescents, 110 young adults, 8 professional clinicians
object_type: LLM-powered human-like AI counseling service (GPT-4o-based concern-aware counseling LLM with visual avatar, voice, and gestures; chunk-based streaming)
evidence_type_tag: Feasibility and user-experience study (cross-sectional, single-session)
modality: LLM-powered conversational agent (GPT-4o-based) with multimodal delivery: text, voice (TTS via ElevenLabs), and visual avatar with gestures and lip-sync. Synchronous, real-time interaction via chunk-based streaming. Audio input via STT (OpenAI Whisper).
session_structure: Single 10-15 minute session in the user study, but designed for multi-session use with session-level context management. Structured counseling phases: initial greetings, exploring client concerns, facilitating problem-solving discussions, and concluding the session. Users can return for additional sessions; conversation context is stored and retrieved.
architecture: Hybrid architecture: deterministic pipeline (STT → counseling LLM → TTS → visual response generation) with generative LLM component (GPT-4o, temperature=0.5, top_p=1.0). Chunk-based streaming with pipelining across modules. Prompt-engineering constrains LLM output with structured counseling techniques and persona.
personalisation: Per-client session-level management storing contextual information and concerns for continuity across visits. Individualized responses based on client's past experiences and previous discussions. Korean-language specific. Face-swapping technology allows user-friendly visual features resembling celebrities or friendly figures. Re-engagement messages for returning clients.
content_corpus: Content corpus derived from two sources: (a) 5 real counseling scripts from actual counseling sessions between a Level 1 Licensed Professional Counselor and students at Seoul National University, and (b) 100 synthetic counseling scripts authored by graduate psychology researchers at Korea University, based on CBT. Real scripts collected via Zoom (~30 min sessions), transcribed via Naver ClovaNote, quality-controlled. Synthetic scripts validated via peer review and professor review with role-play.
interaction_design: Free-text/audio input via speech (STT); open-ended dialogue with structured counseling phases. Counselor persona: 'You are a kind counselor for teenagers.' Conversational and empathetic tone. Summarization and restatement techniques used to demonstrate attentiveness. Automated speech detection with 1-second debouncing for turn-taking. AI counselor performs gestures (nods, note-taking) during responses. Response delivered in 1-second chunks via streaming.
human_support: Fully automated AI counselor; no human involvement during sessions. Professional clinicians participated as evaluators in the user study but not as in-session support. Authors suggest safety guardrails for crisis triage and escalation to human professionals as a policy recommendation, but this is not implemented in the current system.
engagement_features: Re-engagement messages on return (e.g., 'Welcome back! I'm glad to see you again'). Real-time visual indicators showing when speech is being monitored. Automated speech detection removing need for manual microphone activation. Choice of AI counselor visual appearance (celebrity/friendly figure resemblance via face-swapping). AI counselor performs subtle behavioral gestures such as acknowledging nods or note-taking actions.
co_design: Counseling data collected from real sessions (Level 1 Licensed Professional Counselor + students) and synthetic scripts (graduate psychology researchers + professor review). Prompt refined with feedback from psychology experts. Two-step validation for synthetic scripts: peer review followed by professor review with role-play scenarios. User study with 10 adolescents, 110 young adults, and 8 clinicians for feasibility/UX assessment. Expert-driven formative development, not participatory co-design with target end-users.
comparator: comparator_type: active digital | description: Comparative analysis with open-source LLM-based chatbots: ChatCounselor and MentaLLaMA. Each model served as counselor with GPT-4o as client agent across four youth concern scenarios (academic stress, career choices, familial conflicts, interpersonal difficulties). 25 sessions per topic, 100 sessions per model, 10 multi-turn interactions per session. Rated by GPT-4o evaluation agent across 7 domains on 1-5 scale.

personalisation: Context adaptation based on two dimensions of the aggressive message: incivility level (low/moderate/high) and direction of aggression (group-targeted vs individual-targeted). content_corpus: Content derived from psychological theories and empirical evidence; 5 bystander intervention strategies based on established literature

interaction_design: Free-text input or single-choice selection input. The presentation of the chatbot persona was usually presented as a static avatar (n=17). Of these chatbots, 8 were given an anthropomorphic avatar, whether as a photo or drawing (eg, clipart), whereas the rest adopted either a robot, animal, cartoon, or another abstract avatar. human_support: Few studies discussed safeguarding issues. Those that did mentioned they could not provide a person to support the chatbot (conversations with the chatbot are not monitored by a person), so the chatbot was programmed to message the user to contact official health authorities if they had an issue (e.g., directing the user to call 911). engagement_features: The review mentions daily reminders as a feature available to users in some chatbots, and daily notifications for inputting mood data as a confounding factor in intervention design.
co_design: Studies that detailed any user-centered design methodology applied to the development of the chatbot were among the minority (3/32, 9%). One study stands out - the work of Bonnevie and colleagues, who describe the development of Layla through community-based participatory research, where the community that would benefit from the chatbot also had a say in its design. Notable exceptions included 1 study identifying user principles in development; 1 study following a human-centered design process with young adults treated for cancer; and another using community based, participatory research to develop a chatbot.

modality: The review covers conversational AI chatbots across multiple types: rule-based systems (predetermined conversation flows and decision trees), retrieval-based systems (select responses from database), generative AI systems (LLMs like ChatGPT, Claude), and hybrid approaches combining elements. Delivery is primarily text-based dialogue that simulates human conversation; interaction is asynchronous with 24/7 availability.
session_structure: The review reports dose/duration for specific reviewed studies rather than a single intervention. Studies show participants having average of 12 conversations over 2-week periods (Woebot study). Follow-up periods typically 4-8 weeks, with some studies showing improvements maintained at 8-week follow-up. High completion rates (>90%) reported in short-term feasibility studies, but substantial attrition over time in longer-term implementations.
personalisation: The review discusses developmental adaptation requirements including age-appropriate adjustments to conversational complexity, vocabulary, abstract concepts, and interaction patterns across developmental stages. Notes need for cultural responsiveness and linguistic diversity, and adaptation to varying levels of emotional awareness. Current LLMs are noted as trained predominantly on adult-oriented text corpora that poorly represent children's communication patterns.
interaction_design: Text-based dialogue is the primary interaction format that simulates human conversation. Rule-based systems use guided conversations with predetermined flows while generative systems enable more natural, open-ended dialogue. Text-based interactions provide opportunities for reflection and cognitive processing. The perception of non-judgment and anonymity facilitates self-disclosure. The conversational format is noted as feeling more natural and engaging than other digital interventions.
human_support: The literature consistently emphasizes that conversational AI should function as complement to, rather than replacement for, human-delivered mental health support. The most promising implementations position AI within comprehensive ecosystems of care. Hybrid models combining AI and human elements may prove most effective, including AI systems that facilitate connection to human providers or operate under various levels of human supervision. Clear pathways for escalation to human providers are emphasized, particularly for crisis situations.
engagement_features: The review identifies multiple engagement-supporting features: 24/7 availability addressing practical barriers to traditional care, gamification elements (particularly effective for younger children), reminders to enhance compliance with behavioral recommendations, privacy and autonomy features (valued by adolescents), and the conversational/dialogue format itself. Engagement metrics generally exceed non-conversational digital interventions, though substantial attrition remains over time.

modality: This scoping review covers 23 studies of conversational agents (CAs) in healthcare. CA types include rule-based (7 studies), retrieval-based (11 studies), and AI-based (5 studies); 6 integrated affective computing. engagement_features: Reminders mentioned (e.g., TensioBot sends reminders for BP measurement; asthma CA includes medication reminders). personalisation: Four distinct personas (woman in 30s with relationship problems, retired man with chronic pain, teenage boy with bullying, woman grieving loss). Response length adapted (1-2 sentences for reserved/hostile condition). VPs instructed to withhold certain topics until later in conversation. No language-register adaptation or memory across sessions described.
content_corpus: Content corpus was originally designed by the research team based on formative study suggestions from 13 participants (9 peer support volunteers, 4 clinical experts). Clinical assessments used to select symptoms: GAD-7 (anxiety), PHQ-9 (depression), C-SSRS (suicidality), PG-13 (grief), PEG (chronic pain). Testimonials: paracontact approach using NAMI Stigma Free and McLean Hospital Deconstructing Stigma autobiographical stories of African American individuals experiencing depression.
session_structure: Multi-session longitudinal intervention over 14 days. Each session is a 10–15 minute conversation with the ECA. Users can choose the order of sessions. PwD users have 6 core sessions; CM users have 5 core sessions. Users can leave sessions early and resume later, and can revisit completed content. Sessions include: psychoeducation, stigma/self-stigma education, myths & facts quiz, PHQ-8 screening, care-seeking encouragement (PwD only), how to support others (CM only), disclosure education (PwD only), resources, and FAQs.
architecture: Workflow-orchestrated system using custom scripting markup language based on Hierarchical Transition Network Model. Dialogue manager decides state transitions based on user responses and predefined user attributes. Deterministic components with content constraints based on user type assignment. No generative/LLM components. ECA speech via off-the-shelf TTS; nonverbal behavior auto-generated using BEAT.
personalisation: Tailoring by user type (PwD vs CM), stigma status, mental health status (PHQ-8 scores), and cultural/spiritual preferences. Surface-structure tailoring (agent appearance as African American woman) and deep-structure tailoring (Scripture, culturally-relevant health content, racial/ethnic barriers to care). Seven unique faith-based 'getting to know you' scripts. Symptom check-ins tailored to most severe reported PHQ-8 symptom. Resources tailored by user type. However, spiritual tailoring used a one-size-fits-all approach rather than adaptive.
content_corpus: Content corpus was originally developed for this dissertation, drawing on: literature review of stigma-reduction and mental health promotion; self-stigma manualized treatment curriculum (Narrative Enhancement Cognitive Therapy facilitator's manual, Hansson et al., 2017); NAMI Stigma Free campaign testimonials; McLean Hospital Deconstructing Stigma campaign testimonials; Disclosure Processes Model (Chaudoir & Fisher, 2010). Content was adapted through extensive community-engaged co-design across four phases with church members and leaders, and reviewed by a pastor and clinical psychologist.
interaction_design: Menu-based input only — users select from multiple-choice options displayed on screen, updated at each conversational turn. No free-text input. ECA speaks via TTS synchronized with nonverbal behaviors (gaze, gestures, head nods). Dialogue is pre-scripted with constrained, structured pathways. ECA persona is a peer health advisor / church community member. Tone is supportive, non-judgmental, culturally-tailored. ECA provides empathic responses, suggestions, and reflections. Users can skip or choose session order.
human_support: Fully automated ECA system with domain expert review during development. Two domain experts reviewed all sessions: a pastor from one of the churches to validate spiritual elements and a clinical psychologist to determine mental health content met good clinical standards. No human support, clinician involvement, coach, peer support, or moderation during actual intervention delivery.
engagement_features: Daily symptom check-ins for users with positive symptoms, choice of session order (user-selected sequence), ability to revisit completed content, resources can be sent via SMS to user's phone, culturally-tailored content to increase relevance, Scripture and religious content for motivation, community-building framing to encourage engagement
co_design: Extensive multi-phase community-engaged co-design over 4+ years. Phase I: 3 discussion-based focus groups (11 key informants) exploring community context, social support, technology use. Phase II: 4 participatory design focus groups using affinity diagramming, drawing/writing, dialogue tailoring worksheets, modular storyboards, and Photovoice. Phase III: 28-day field deployment of Church Connect (25 participants) with follow-up interviews. Phase IV: individual interviews with 8 church leaders using depression storyboards for feature selection. Methods included participatory design, CBPR principles, asset-based approaches. Changes made: CBT removed after stakeholder discomfort; spiritual tailoring integrated based on co-design; ECA appearance/persona co-designed.

title: Applications of Large Language Models in the Field of Suicide Prevention: Scoping Review.
bibliographic: authors: Glenn Holmes, Biya Tang, Sunil Gupta, Svetha Venkatesh, Helen Christensen, Alexis Whitton | year: 2025 | title: Applications of Large Language Models in the Field of Suicide Prevention: Scoping Review | venue: J Med Internet Res | doi: 10.2196/63126 | publication_type: journal article
sample_size: basis: included studies for synthesis | n_studies: 43
object_type: Large language models (LLMs) - various types including BERT, GPT, and other transformer-based models for suicide prevention applications
evidence_type_tag: Scoping review of LLM applications in suicide prevention
modality: Across the 43 included studies, modalities included text-based chatbot/conversational interfaces (e.g., ChatGPT), question-and-answer interfaces, and classification/detection systems applied to social media text. Of 9 generative applications, 7 used the text-based ChatGPT user interface and 2 used text-based interfaces for an educational BERT model and a data-secure FLAN model. One study used an LLM for image interpretation. Most studies (33/43) used LLMs for contextual language understanding (classification/detection), not interactive delivery.
architecture: Most studies (35/43, 81%) used BERT or a fine-tuned BERT variant for contextual understanding/classification tasks. GPT models were used in 9/43 (21%) studies, primarily for generative applications. In 33/43 (77%) studies, LLMs were used for contextual language understanding (deterministic classification); 9/43 (21%) used generative capabilities. The review notes guardrails are needed: 'models of LLM use in crisis support contexts are most likely to be those that are driven by clinical oversight, with sufficient guardrails in place to trigger referrals when clinically indicated.'
content_corpus: Social media was the most common source of LLM training data (31/43, 72%), with Reddit (18/43, 42%) and X/Twitter (13/43, 30%) most common. Other sources included crisis counseling app/service data (3 studies), National Violent Death Report System data, educational/academic documents, participant vignettes, research participant data, and direct prompt inputs to ChatGPT. One educational interface drew on 'a corpus of >300 suicide-specific documents curated by clinicians.'
interaction_design: Generative applications used text-based interfaces, including the ChatGPT user interface and custom text-based interfaces. One study developed a question-and-answer interface for suicide prevention information. Another prompted ChatGPT with sequential PHQ-9 items to simulate a patient with escalating suicide risk. Another asked ChatGPT to generate mental health nurse care plans from vignettes. The review notes LLMs can 'simulate empathy' but 'lack the authenticity and relational aspects required for modern mental health care.'
human_support: The review emphasizes human-in-the-loop oversight as essential. Proposed models include clinician copilot systems, clinical oversight with guardrails for referral, and expert external validation. No included study deployed a fully automated standalone intervention; applications were either classification/detection tools, proposed future clinical assistance tools, or pilot studies. The review states LLMs 'should not replace clinical judgment but rather supplement it' and recommends 'human-in-the-loop testing or expert external validation.'

Intent classifier training data: 8400 anonymized utterances from online sleep-related communities (r/insomnia, r/sleepdisorders), rewritten using GPT-4o mini, annotated with CBT-I techniques, augmented to ~2000 samples per technique. RAG dataset: 217 expert-curated counseling pairs from publicly available online counseling resources, manually reviewed and labeled.

Model generates structured outputs: empathic acknowledgment, question type, subquestion, and depth-control signal. Tone: empathic acknowledgment followed by probing questions encouraging hypothesis testing rather than directive correction. Users may accept, defer, or select alternative technique. human_support: Fully automated system with no human support during sessions. System explicitly not designed for clinical diagnosis, treatment, or crisis intervention. Depth-control signal in Socratic questioning regulates conversational pacing.

session_structure: Repeated sessions over 30 days (1 month) with varied weekly topics. Five steps: (1) observing oneself, (2) understanding strengths and weaknesses while working, (3) establishing personalized strategies by reflecting on behavioral patterns, (4) learning effective strategies, (5) reflecting on personal change. Participants instructed to use at least 3-4 times a week for a month (required use period), followed by a 1-month free use period.
architecture: Hybrid orchestration: predetermined scenario framework with generative model components. Two primary algorithms: (1) response-generating algorithm (answer classifier using Korean BERT classifies user responses as uncertain/skeptical/normal; answer generator using Korean GPT-2 fine-tuned for the scenario generates responses), and (2) procrastination factor algorithm (multilayered CNN classifier detecting 6 procrastination factors to provide tailored advice). Deterministic scenario flow with generative responses within each step. Content restricted to procrastination-related topics.
personalisation: Tailored advice based on detected procrastination factors (6 factors: physical and emotional stress, social relationships, environmental distractions, perfectionism, low self-regulation, lack of motivation). If user disagrees with inferred top factor, second-highest factor advice is recommended and the matrix is updated. Responses generated are tailored to user utterances. Chatbot initiates conversation based on the user's success rate from the to-do app.
content_corpus: Content corpus sourced from: (1) survey data collected from 447 undergraduate students (2021-2022) via open-ended questionnaires, elaborated for training; (2) open-source wellness conversation script dataset from AI Hub (765 sentence pairs selected). Total 18,453 sentences used for fine-tuning the answer generator; 3356 sentences for answer classifier; 719 sentences for procrastination factor classifier.
interaction_design: Mixed input: free-text user responses classified by the answer classifier into uncertain, skeptical, or normal categories. Scenario-based dialogue with predetermined questions; generative responses within each scenario step. Interrogative sentences from the generator prompt further user response; declarative sentences advance to the next scenario step. Tone described as 'cute and friendly' by users. Chatbot provides advice, feedback, consolation/cheering, and conversation for reflection. Users can disagree with inferred procrastination factors, triggering alternative advice.
human_support: Fully automated. No clinician, coach, or peer support during use. Clinical psychologists (4 certified) were involved only in content development (providing advice for the database). engagement_features: Push alarms in the morning and evening to remind participants to make lists and complete daily tasks. In the treatment group, a Moa message accompanied the evening push alarm. Calendar visualization of success rate. Success rate automatically calculated as ratio of checked lists to total lists. Participants required to use at least 3-4 times per week during the required use period; disqualification if use requirements not met for a particular week. Compensation based on duration of involvement.

architecture: Heterogeneous architectures across studies: hybrid approaches combining rule-based reliability with LLM/GPT adaptability are highlighted as most promising. Dr. Joy: semantic similarity matching to Q&A sets. Users consistently desire more personalized responses. Review recommends future chatbots strive for greater personalization including context-specific responses and adjusting responses to prioritize key concerns.

Some CAs were culture-specific (4/39, 10%) or gender-specific (3/39, 8%). One study found youth preferred choosing from 3-4 characters with variations of gender, avatar, age, and social role rather than personalizing each aspect separately.
content_corpus: Content corpus was built upon expert knowledge in all studies (39/39, 100%). CBT-based content (19/39, 49%), positive psychology (7/39, 18%), other therapeutic content (7/39, 18%), and clinical expert knowledge from school health service experts or counselors (6/39, 15%). In 4/39 (10%), the source was not specified. One study used positive answers collected from a web forum. A few incorporated inputs from youth.
